newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan stocks seen up on election, fundamentals.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan stocks seen up on election, fundamentals.

text.p: Pakistan's economy may not recover immediately, but Nawaz Sharif's convincing election victory early this month could boost the stock market over the next 12 months, analysts said on Thursday.
"We do not foresee a miraculous economic recovery immediately but Nawaz Sharif does inspire confidence among investors," Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said.
He said the Pakistani stock market was quite attractive on fundamentals.
Sharif, prime minister-elect, easily won the February 3 general elections and said he expected to take power February 17.

Analysts said the macro-economic situation might not improve soon but the market believed that Sharif, who has repeatedly vowed to keep the revival of the economy as his top priority, would be able to fulfil his financial goals.
The consumer price index rose 2.17 percent in January compared to December, representing a year-on-year increase of 13.4 percent, up from 11.41 percent in December and 8.93 percent in January 1996.
Exports fell 18.6 percent to a provisional $652 million in January from $801 million in December, and were down 20.9 percent when compared to exports of $824 million in January 1996.
Imports dropped 1.3 percent to $1.028 billion in January from $1.042 billion in December, but increased by 10.4 percent compared to January 1996's figure of $931 million.
The trade gap rose to a provisional $2.126 billion in the first seven months of the 1996/97 (July-June) financial year from $2.097 billion in the year-ago period.

The analysts said fuel price increases, which are linked to international prices, and higher consumption during the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, seemed to spur the rise. Gas rates rose 26.5 percent in January and kerosene 4.75 percent.
Aziz said the decline in exports was due to an overall slump in trade activity because of the elections and Ramadan, which ended on February 8.
Analyst Nadeem Naqvi of International Asset Management Co Ltd said the drop in exports could be linked to a 7.86 percent devaluation of the rupee against the dollar in October.
"Exporters had booked a lot of orders following the October devaluation. They had to take a breather," he said, adding that the situation would soon normalise and exports would pick up.
Naqvi predicted the stock market would rise to 1,900 within the next 12 months if Sharif sped up privatisation and enforced financial discipline.
At 0900 GMT, the Karachi Stock Exchange index was at 1,623.53 points, down 1.17 percent, or 19.19 points, on selling of blue chips.
"The important thing is that Pakistan's socio-political risk factor has dropped significantly after Sharif's victory."

He said Sharif's election win had changed investor perception about Pakistan's future and could help bring back an estimated two to four billion dollars of capital that left in 1995 and 1996 because of political uncertainty.
